title: Do Not Blame a Heart That Softens or Is Led Captive
intro: Alqimmah Studio dates this poem to Ihab al-Shabatat's first visit to Damascus, in early June 2026. He had mourned Syria under Assad. Now the scent of jasmine welcomes him to the city and brings back the young people who died. He passes through its gates into the streets of al-Qaymariyya, then follows the memory of the Umayyad capital west to al-Andalus.

translation: Do not blame a heart that softens or is led captive.
Its spirit has seen Damascus and breathed its scent.
1.sharh: The visitor comes to know the city through sight and smell. A small movement in the sound of raqqa, “grew tender”, produces riqq, “bondage”, as though tenderness itself had put him in chains.

translation: Why did you spare all the others your reproach?
They met before him what he meets now.
2.sharh: The accuser would have to reproach everyone who came here before him. What looks like a private weakness turns out to be a shared experience.

translation: No soul has ever gone away from her
without a collar of longing gracing its neck.
3.sharh: The soul can leave Damascus wearing its longing like a necklace. The ring around its neck preserves something of the captivity in the opening, yet the traveller is proud to show it.

translation: Why blame him if he finds delight
in Syria's bonds and wishes for no release?
4.sharh: What would normally be a captive's strongest wish, being set free, now seems an unwelcome prospect. The bondage is his attachment to staying in the city.

translation: Human fellowship has its root in Damascus,
with branches in sight to west and east.
5.sharh: He imagines the settled life people share as a tree rooted in Damascus. Western and eastern cities belong to the same tree as its far-reaching branches.

translation: She breathes jasmine. Love moistens
her lips with coquetry, wineskin after wineskin.
6.sharh: Jasmine is the city's breath. Her charm then becomes something liquid which Love can pour at her lips, drawing on one whole wineskin after another.

translation: Morning kisses her mouth when it rises over her,
sharing it with night, one corner of her lips apiece.
7.sharh: Dawn and night approach the same mouth from opposite sides. Their division of a day becomes the sharing of a kiss.

translation: From them come our darkness and our light,
like two lovers who cannot bear to part.
8.sharh: Twilight lets the observer see what is left of night beside the first light. In this brief overlap they look like lovers trying to lengthen a farewell.

translation: God split the dawn for the business of the day
and set her apart from the enchantment of the East.
9.sharh: The separation of dawn from darkness gives people a day in which to act. Damascus, too, is singled out from among the other places that make the East enchanting.

translation: Civilisations have come one after another upon her
like clouds passing over a clear watering place.
10.sharh: Empires pass like cloud cover. What holds the eye is the clear water beneath them, still available after the shadows overhead have changed.

translation: Time itself seems one of her lovers.
The world grows old. Her age stands still.
11.sharh: Time is pictured pausing in admiration. Everything else continues to age while the city it has stopped to look at keeps the same face.

translation: In her youth, though nights have turned her grey,
my Lord's command can lift what lay below.
12.sharh: Nights here count both years and ordeals. Their marks can be real while the city still has a future, since God can overturn the order of things.

translation: If people mourn her in words of flame,
she rises from their ashes like the phoenix.
13.sharh: Even the elegy meant to pronounce her dead supplies the ashes from which she rises. The Arabic anqa takes on the phoenix's familiar power of rebirth.

translation: Swords took Damascus's name to perfect their own,
heedless of more fire and hammering.
14.sharh: The name Damascus is itself a mark of excellence for a blade. The sword is imagined accepting each further blow of the smith's hammer to earn the name.

translation: She and the sword are kin in rhyme. When it longs,
it slips from its sheath to meet its love.
15.sharh: As the sword slips free, the sounds at the join between ghimd and mashqan almost release the name Dimashq, Damascus. The sword's home has found a place inside its rhyme.

translation: Damascus is a bunch of grapes from a vine
I carry in my heart. I grow drunk on longing.
16.sharh: The grapes are carried inward rather than eaten. As grapes can ferment with time, keeping the city in his heart leaves him drunk on the longing it has produced.

translation: Or the glad tidings of a dove after a long absence,
bearing dawn on its wings for one who lived in darkness.
17.sharh: The city becomes the good news long awaited by someone who has lived through darkness. The wings of the returning bird open out like daybreak.

translation: Zenobia's pride is in the parting of her hair.
Al-Sarout's blood sets a horizon aglow.
18.sharh: A queen from ancient Syria gives the city her proud bearing, a protest singer of modern Homs the red light on its horizon. They stand in the same portrait despite the centuries between them.

translation: How I grieve for those flowers of youth
that death smelt. If only it had spared that breath.
19.sharh: What attracted him to Damascus now frightens him. Death is imagined stopping to smell the young people as casually as a passer-by might bend over flowers.

translation: Patience, my grieving heart, as death plucks one soul
after another, their nectar flowing in a rush.
20.sharh: Death moves on from smelling the flowers to picking them. Their nectar runs all at once, recalling the blood of the young people without naming it again.

translation: The scent of flowers never made me shudder
until I lost you. Now I smell them and suffer.
21.sharh: Loss has changed what a scent does to his body. The same flowers that welcomed him to the city can now make his skin shiver.

translation: Whenever I smell flowers, I am like
a hanged man's mother at the sight of a rope.
22.sharh: A rope need only come into the mother's sight for an entire loss to return. That involuntary recognition is what the scent of flowers now does to him.

translation: Glory appeared as a bee flying up towards you.
You rise into the sky, and it rises after you.
23.sharh: The bee follows the nectar. By letting the dead rise first and glory follow at their heels, he gives them the power to confer honour even on glory itself.

translation: It need only have slept in the graves
that held you. How could they cramp it?
24.sharh: The bee's ascent gives way to a resting place below ground. If those graves could contain people of such stature, glory itself could find room there.

translation: God the Merciful give peace to those companions,
with the loftiest angels for their company.
25.sharh: He replaces the image of separate graves with one of fellowship. The word for companions in the first half finds its answer in the company of angels in the second.

translation: May he grant you a sweet meeting with gardens,
for you were the finest cluster among people.
26.sharh: The dead are the finest fruit their people bore. A date cluster suits both the prayer for a garden and the idea of a generation held together on one stem.

translation: Would that I were with your spirits in those gardens,
like doves beneath the leaves of a great tree.
27.sharh: Once more he pictures a group of birds, this time at rest. The wish is for the safety of sharing shelter with the people he has been mourning.

translation: Criminal hands would never have stretched so far
without hypocritical palms closing in applause.
28.sharh: Two movements of the hand expose two responsibilities. One reaches out to do harm while the others come together in applause.

translation: Tomorrow God's hand will judge those hands,
as though the victims' eyes had seen no calamity.
29.sharh: All the hands in the previous line come under one judgement. He imagines redress so complete that those who suffered might feel they had never witnessed disaster.

translation: These words were tears held fast in my eyes,
until my tongue asked them for a drink.
30.sharh: The verses have a source as physical as a spring. Tears that never fell from the eyes reach the tongue instead and come out as speech.

translation: My eyes are clouds in the sky,
raining on my tongue when it goes dry.
31.sharh: An inability to speak becomes a drought. The tears work like rain on dry ground, letting words grow where his tongue had fallen silent.

translation: Perhaps the soul itself gives entry to the door
in the wall it has kept trying to pierce.
32.sharh: He has just found words by drawing upon his own tears. The inward discovery suggests that the soul may already contain the way through an obstacle it has been attacking from outside.

translation: I entered Damascus through her seven gates,
giving thanks for our meeting with the seven oft-repeated verses.
33.sharh: The traditional seven gates of Damascus meet a second seven, the verses of the opening chapter of the Quran. Reciting them makes his entry both an arrival and a thanksgiving.

translation: Afterwards she opened a gate into poetry
and showed me gazelles pushing at its bolt.
34.sharh: After the seven real entrances comes one only a poet can use. The poems behind it have the swift, elusive bodies of gazelles and might shut him out again.

translation: I was quick with the straight arrow and hit
what gives the ear delight in delicacy and taste.
35.sharh: His quarry is a verse that sounds right. Hunting supplies the urgency and precision, the listener's ear the test of whether his aim was true.

translation: My two friends, hurry me on my way.
A longing heart is quicker to drive me.
36.sharh: He borrows the traditional address to two travelling companions. Neither can set a faster pace than the longing that is already driving him on.

translation: My footsteps keep time with my heart's verse,
as though my heart weighed out each beat.
37.sharh: A footfall, a heartbeat and a foot of verse come to keep the same time. The Arabic verb for weighing also belongs to the language of poetic metre.

translation: No full moon rivals the moons of al-Qaymariyya.
Outside Damascus can you truly glimpse the moon?
38.sharh: The moons are people in the old neighbourhood where he stayed. After seeing their faces, the literal moon seems to him a less convincing example of what poets mean by beauty.

translation: You know her people by their features,
the brightest faces and the finest speech.
39.sharh: The claim is personal and sensory. After the faces that drew his eye come the voices by which he recognises the same people even in conversation.

translation: The eye's glance stirs an opinion in you.
The spirit's visions make the truth clear to you.
40.sharh: The outer eye can give a first impression of a face. To know what those faces mean to him, the visitor needs the inward sight the next line calls love between hearts.

translation: The heart's desire for bodies is a passing impulse.
Its desire for hearts is the clearer love.
41.sharh: The word for the first attraction suggests a sudden leap. A love that has found another heart gives him firmer grounds for calling the feeling love.

translation: I grew attached to Syria as home and people,
a fish that dies choking without its water.
42.sharh: He has become so dependent on the place and its people that a visit no longer feels optional. The fish gasping outside its water gives homesickness a bodily measure.

translation: Their guest takes them for young attendants in paradise.
Foes imagine them blue jinn.
43.sharh: A guest sees the gracious attendants of paradise. An enemy sees fierce otherworldly beings. The same people inspire the two wildly different visions.

translation: Their pride in shunning disgrace is as great as Iblis's.
On the field of battle it outruns lightning.
44.sharh: Iblis is proverbial for pride at its furthest extreme. The poet borrows its magnitude and gives it a different object, a refusal to stoop to disgrace.

translation: Are you not the people of whom a prophet said,
if you went wrong, no good would return to mankind?
45.sharh: He alludes to a saying of Muhammad that makes the moral condition of Syria's people a measure of the wider community. It raises the stakes of the praise he has been offering them.

translation: I wonder about the visitor and the visited.
Does a branch with roots sunk deep ever wither?
46.sharh: Visitor and city seem to belong to a single tree. The deep root continues to nourish a branch that might have taken its own distance for estrangement.

translation: I have never embraced Damascus without feeling
the breeze of Jordan all around me, its exact match.
47.sharh: The breeze makes kinship almost palpable. To this visitor it feels the same on both sides of the border, right down to the way it passes over him.

translation: The bowls of our eyes are full of tears
for little neighbours dead through distance and burning.
48.sharh: The “little neighbours” are neighbouring towns, according to the studio's gloss. Eyes become great collecting bowls for grief over places lost through destruction or estrangement.

translation: I gave thanks for the blessing granted Damascus.
What provision can there be beyond freedom today?
49.sharh: After grieving for other towns, he can give thanks for the change he believes he has lived to see in this one. Freedom enters his vocabulary as a gift sustaining life.

translation: I no longer see the Russians' swagger entrenched,
or hear the Persians follow their blows with braying.
50.sharh: The visitor describes the passing of Russian and Iranian power in deliberately abusive terms. A play on Rus and raws supplies the first insult, an animal sound the second.

translation: The spearpoint takes no blame, Roman or Persian,
when the Arabs' own points stand far apart.
51.sharh: Calling the foreign spear Roman or Persian draws on an older language of rivalry. What he faults here is the scattering of the spearheads on his own side.

translation: Many an owl has gone and left its chicks.
Word of a feast spread. They greeted people with a croak.
52.sharh: The owls stand for the old regime and its backers in the studio gloss. Their political heirs answer a day of public celebration with the least festive greeting imaginable.

translation: What harm if they had only kept quiet
when Su'da came briefly visiting with her joyful cry?
53.sharh: Su'da, a woman's name that suggests good fortune, gives fleeting happiness a voice. The owls could at least let her celebratory ululation be heard.

translation: Truly these lands, whose people are Umayya's,
are bound to Arab kinship by the firmest ties.
54.sharh: A handhold is literally something one can grasp. The image makes the old Umayyad identity of Damascus a bond with the wider Arab world that the speaker can still hold onto.

translation: Who equates the woman who suckled a man on rancour
with one whose hands encircled a neck in generosity?
55.sharh: The rival legacies are women in the act of giving something to another person. One nourishes spite, the other's arms make an encircling gesture of generosity.

translation: Even without a sword the hands of Umayya
came close to cutting a throat in war.
56.sharh: The image tests the strength of the dynasty in the poet's imagination by first taking its weapon away. The hands that bestowed gifts a line ago now represent power in war.

translation: Greatness and Umayya were sewn into one,
and the Lord never decreed they should be torn apart.
57.sharh: The Quran's account of heaven and earth joined and then parted supplies the opposed words. The poet changes the outcome for the pair he is celebrating.

translation: Whoever aims base charges at Umayya
has his folly sent back towards his head by the bow.
58.sharh: A charge against the dynasty becomes an arrow whose bow perversely shoots backwards. It is the accuser's judgement that the poet puts on trial.

translation: May God whiten the eye that disowns the one
who joined the green land's patches and stretched them deep.
59.sharh: The whitened eye is an imprecation of blindness. Against that loss of sight he sets a vividly visible patchwork, the lands brought under one rule in his account of Umayyad power.

translation: From Damascus her banners bore al-Andalus,
one half of the world's two horizons taken into their fold.
60.sharh: Al-Andalus marks the western reach of a caliphate centred in Damascus. The curious expression “the two Easts” brings both ends of the inhabited world into the line.

translation: East and West will see that Damascus
is their finest soil, with the finest stock upon it.
61.sharh: The judgement works upwards, from the ground of the city to the ancestry of its people. It rounds off a poem that began with just one visitor reporting what his own senses told him.

1.1.4.meaning: To soften or grow tender. Its sound is echoed in the word for bondage.

1.1.7.head: رِقّ
1.1.7.meaning: Bondage or enslavement to the city he loves.

1.2.4.head: دِمَشق
1.2.4.meaning: Damascus, the Syrian capital, also called al-Sham and al-Fayha in this poem.

2.1.3.head: عَذَلَ
2.1.3.meaning: To reproach, especially a lover for the object of his devotion.

3.2.1.head: جيد
3.2.1.meaning: A neck, especially one seen as adorned.

3.2.3.head: صَبابَة
3.2.3.meaning: The tenderness and ache of longing.

5.1.1.head: مَألَف
5.1.1.meaning: A familiar gathering place or home.

6.2.2.head: دَلّ
6.2.2.meaning: Coquetry or winning grace in one's bearing.

6.2.4.head: زِقّ
6.2.4.meaning: A leather skin used to hold wine or other drink.

7.1.3.head: ثَغر
7.1.3.meaning: The mouth or the front teeth seen in a smile.

7.2.4.head: شِدق
7.2.4.meaning: One corner or side of the mouth.

10.2.5.meaning: A place where water is drawn or drunk.

11.2.5.head: رَوق
11.2.5.meaning: The prime of a thing. The studio gloss takes it here as the city's unchanged age.

12.1.4.head: شابَ
12.1.4.meaning: To go grey, said here of the city under the strain of its nights.

13.2.4.head: العَنقاء
13.2.4.meaning: Al-anqa, a fabulous bird of Arabic lore. Here it rises like a phoenix from its ashes.

14.1.2.head: تَدَمشَقَ
14.1.2.meaning: To become Damascene, here said of swords acquiring their famous place-name.

15.2.5-6.head: الغِمد مَشقاً
15.2.5-6.meaning: “From the sheath, drawn swiftly”. The sounds d-m-sh-q across the words recall Dimashq, Damascus.

16.1.4.head: حَمَلَ
16.1.4.meaning: “I carry it”. The metre divides the word ahmiluhu across the two halves.

17.1.2.meaning: An affectionate diminutive of good tidings.

18.1.2.head: الزَّبّاء
18.1.2.meaning: Al-Zabba', the queen of Arabic tradition associated with Zenobia of third-century Palmyra.

18.2.2.head: السّاروت
18.2.2.meaning: Abdel-Basset al-Sarout, a goalkeeper and protest singer from Homs who died of battle wounds in 2019.

19.2.5.head: نَشق
19.2.5.meaning: Drawing a scent into the nostrils.

20.1.2.head: وَجد
20.1.2.meaning: Deep feeling, here anguish for those who were killed.

22.2.6.head: حَدَق
22.2.6.meaning: Gazing or fixing one's eyes. The mother's clear sight of the rope prompts the memory.

23.1.5.head: عَلا
23.1.5.meaning: “Rises”. The verb ta'lu continues in the second half.

24.2.3.head: زَوى
24.2.3.meaning: To draw in, compress or confine.

25.2.1.head: الأُلى
25.2.1.meaning: An old relative pronoun meaning “those who”.

26.2.5.head: عِذق
26.2.5.meaning: A date cluster hanging from a palm, here a figure for shared stock.

29.2.5.head: بَوق
29.2.5.meaning: A calamity or severe affliction, the sense the studio gives this word.

30.2.5.meaning: To ask for water, here the tongue asking the eyes for their tears.

33.1.2-3.head: الأَبواب السَّبعَة
33.1.2-3.meaning: “The seven gates”, the traditional gates of the walled Old City of Damascus, including Bab Tuma and Bab Sharqi.

33.2.2-3.head: السَّبع المَثاني
33.2.2-3.meaning: “The seven oft-repeated”, a Quranic name understood here as al-Fatiha, the seven verses opening the Quran.

34.2.4.head: غَلق
34.2.4.meaning: The closing of a door or the fastening that holds it shut.

36.1.1.head: خَليلان
36.1.1.meaning: “My two friends”, a traditional address to companions in Arabic verse.

37.1.5.meaning: In accord, here footsteps matching a pulse.

38.1.3.head: القيمَرِيَّة
38.1.3.meaning: Al-Qaymariyya, a neighbourhood of Old Damascus where the studio says the poet stayed.

39.1.1.head: سيما
39.1.1.meaning: A distinguishing mark or the look by which a face is recognised.

39.1.4.head: أَبهى
39.1.4.meaning: “More radiant”. The word abha straddles the two halves.

42.1.2.head: الشَّآم
42.1.2.meaning: Al-Sha'm, a form of al-Sham, the historical Syrian region and a name for its city of Damascus.

43.1.3-4.head: غِلمان خُلد
43.1.3-4.meaning: “Youths of eternity”, the youthful attendants described in Quranic accounts of paradise.

44.1.2.head: إِبليس
44.1.2.meaning: Iblis, who in the Quran refuses out of pride to bow to Adam.

44.2.2.meaning: The din of battle, and hence battle itself.

45.1.3-4.meaning: “If you go wrong”, a reference to the prophetic saying transmitted by al-Tirmidhi about the people of Syria.

46.1.1-2.meaning: “Would that I knew”, an old formula for wondering about something.

46.2.2.meaning: To wither or shrivel, of living growth.

47.1.3.head: الفَيحاء
47.1.3.meaning: Al-Fayha, an epithet of Damascus, literally a spacious tract.

48.1.1.head: جَفنَة
48.1.1.meaning: Large bowls. Jifan also brings the similar word for eyelid, jafn, to mind.

48.2.1.head: جُوَيرَة
48.2.1.meaning: “Little neighbours”, neighbouring Arab towns in the studio's explanation.

50.1.5.head: رَوس
50.1.5.meaning: Swagger or a fault. Raws repeats the sounds of Rus, “the Russians”.

50.2.5.head: نَهق
50.2.5.meaning: A donkey's braying, used here as an insult.

51.2.1.head: أَسُنّ
51.2.1.meaning: Points or teeth, the plural of sinn, set against the single foreign spearpoint.

53.2.1.head: زَغرَدَ
53.2.1.meaning: To ululate, giving a high trilling cry of celebration.

53.2.2.meaning: Su'da, a woman's name related to good fortune, here fleeting joy personified.

54.1.2.head: أُمَيَّة
54.1.2.meaning: Umayya, the ancestor who gives the Umayyad dynasty its name. His descendants ruled from Damascus.

54.1.4.head: أَمتَن
54.1.4.meaning: “Firmest”. The comparative amtan is divided at the caesura.

54.2.2.head: عُروَة
54.2.2.meaning: A loop or handhold, hence a secure bond.

57.1.5.head: رَتق
57.1.5.meaning: “Joined up”. Ratqan is divided across the halves and answered by fatqan, a tearing apart.

59.1.1-3.head: بَيَّضَ اللَّه عَينَهُ
59.1.1-3.meaning: “May God whiten his eye”, a curse of blindness.

59.2.2-3.head: رُقَع الخَضراء
59.2.2-3.meaning: “The patches of the green land”, territories pictured as patches of one garment.

59.2.5.head: غَمق
59.2.5.meaning: Depth or penetration inland, paired with the joining of territories.

60.1.5.head: أَندَلُس
60.1.5.meaning: Al-Andalus, the historical Muslim territories of the Iberian Peninsula. The place-name runs across the caesura.

60.2.3.head: المَشرِقان
60.2.3.meaning: “The two Easts”, here East and West taken together under one name.

60.2.4.head: اِستَشَقَّ
60.2.4.meaning: To take or set on one side. The studio links the verb to shiqq, a half or side.

61.2.5.head: عِرق
61.2.5.meaning: Stock or descent, referring the praise of the soil back to its people.
